q: Cumulative incidence (incidence risk) measures:
o: The proportion of a population with disease at one point in time
The proportion of at-risk individuals who develop disease over a defined period
The number of deaths among confirmed cases
e: Cumulative incidence is the proportion of an at-risk group developing new disease over a stated period; a measure of risk.

q: Incidence rate (incidence density) differs from cumulative incidence because its denominator is:
o: The total population at one time point
e: Incidence rate uses animal-time at risk, giving cases per unit time and accommodating varying follow-up.

q: When calculating cumulative incidence of an in-shelter disease, which animals must be EXCLUDED from the at-risk denominator?
o: Animals over six months of age
Animals already infected at the start and those arriving already infected
e: The denominator includes only animals capable of developing new disease, so existing and incoming cases are excluded.

q: Screening every cat for FeLV on intake day and reporting the proportion already infected measures:
e: Disease present at a single time point in a population is point prevalence.

q: A chronic, long-duration disease tends to have:
o: Low prevalence relative to its incidence
High prevalence relative to its incidence
e: Prevalence is approximately incidence times duration, so long-duration disease accumulates a high prevalence.

q: August intake is 111 cats, 6 arriving already infected. The Aug 1 resident census is 39, of which 11 are infected and 3 recovered before Aug 1. The population at risk is:
e: Incoming at risk 111 minus 6 = 105; resident at risk 39 minus 11 minus 3 = 25; total 130.

q: Which measure best expresses the probability that an individual animal will develop a disease?
e: Incidence captures new disease over time, the measure of individual risk; prevalence reflects existing burden.

q: Why is the incidence rate (animal-time) often preferred over simple cumulative incidence in shelters?
o: It is easier to calculate by hand
Shelter populations are unstable with widely varying lengths of stay
e: Animal-time denominators handle the variable follow-up created by differing lengths of stay.

q: In a cohort study, relative risk is calculated as:
o: The odds of exposure in cases divided by controls
Incidence in the exposed divided by incidence in the unexposed
Existing cases divided by total population
e: Relative risk is the ratio of incidence in exposed to unexposed, available from cohort designs.

q: The odds ratio from a case-control study approximates the relative risk when:
e: Under the rare-disease assumption the odds ratio approximates the relative risk.

q: A relative risk of 1.0 indicates:
o: No association between exposure and outcome
e: For a ratio measure the null value is 1, meaning no association.

q: The absolute excess risk in the exposed group compared with the unexposed is the:
e: Attributable risk is the difference in incidence between exposed and unexposed, an absolute measure.

q: A 2x2 table shows exposed cases 40, exposed non-cases 60, unexposed cases 20, unexposed non-cases 80. The relative risk is:
e: Risk exposed 40/100 = 0.4; risk unexposed 20/100 = 0.2; RR = 0.4/0.2 = 2.0.

q: An odds ratio is statistically non-significant when its 95% confidence interval includes:
e: Ratio measures have a null value of 1; an interval that includes 1 is not significant.

q: A relative risk of 0.6 for a vaccinated group indicates:
e: A relative risk below 1 indicates reduced risk, here a protective effect.

q: In a shelter trial, URI incidence is 30% in unvaccinated cats and 10% in vaccinated cats. The number needed to treat (NNT) is:
e: ARR = 30% − 10% = 0.20. NNT = 1 ÷ ARR = 1 ÷ 0.20 = 5. Five cats must be vaccinated to prevent one URI case.

q: Number Needed to Treat (NNT) is derived from which statistic?
e: NNT = 1 ÷ ARR. Using the absolute risk difference means two interventions with the same RR can still have very different NNTs if their baseline risks differ.

q: Dividing the number of animals that die of a disease by the number of confirmed cases of that disease gives the:
e: Case fatality rate uses confirmed cases as its denominator and reflects disease severity.

q: The denominator of the crude mortality rate is:
o: The total population at risk of dying
e: Crude mortality uses the whole at-risk population, not just cases.

q: Which statement correctly distinguishes case fatality rate from mortality rate?
o: Mortality rate uses cases as the denominator
Case fatality rate uses cases as the denominator; mortality rate uses the whole population
e: The key difference is the denominator: cases for case fatality rate, whole population for mortality rate.

q: The number of deaths from parvovirus divided by the total population at risk during the interval is the:
e: Cause-specific mortality isolates deaths from one disease over the whole at-risk population.

q: Ten dogs are confirmed with parvovirus and four die. The case fatality rate is:
e: Case fatality rate = 4 deaths / 10 cases = 40%.

q: Morbidity in a population is best described by:
o: The proportion of positive diagnostic tests
The incidence or prevalence of illness
e: Morbidity refers to the occurrence of illness, captured by incidence or prevalence.

q: The proportion of the total shelter population that dies from any cause during a period is the:
e: All-cause death over the whole population is the crude mortality rate.

q: A surveillance system in which the shelter actively seeks out cases rather than waiting for reports is:
e: Active surveillance involves deliberately seeking cases; passive relies on cases being reported in.

q: In the population approach to disease, the equivalent of forming a differential diagnosis for an individual is:
o: Performing a physical exam on each animal
Formulating epidemiological hypotheses about disease frequency
e: At the population level the clinician forms hypotheses to explain the observed frequency and distribution of disease.

q: A disease consistently present at a stable, expected baseline level in a population is described as:
e: Endemic refers to the usual expected baseline level; an excess above that is an epidemic or outbreak.

q: An epidemic curve with a single sharp peak, cases clustered within one incubation period, suggests:
e: A single sharp peak within one incubation period is the signature of a common point-source exposure.

q: Successive peaks of cases spaced about one incubation period apart on an epidemic curve suggest:
e: Progressive waves spaced by the incubation period indicate animal-to-animal propagated spread.

q: The primary purpose of establishing a case definition early in an outbreak investigation is to:
o: Count cases consistently across the investigation
e: A standard case definition lets investigators count cases consistently in time, place and animal.

q: Attack rates calculated for different subgroups during an outbreak are used mainly to:
o: Identify which groups are at highest risk
e: Comparing attack rates across subgroups highlights the highest-risk groups and points to the source.

q: The sensitivity of a surveillance system refers to:
o: The proportion of true cases it detects
e: Surveillance sensitivity is the proportion of actual cases the system successfully detects.

q: Which of the following is a true ratio but NOT a proportion?
e: A proportion requires the numerator to be a subset of the denominator. A sex ratio compares two independent groups, neither of which is a subset of the other, so it is a ratio but not a proportion.

q: What distinguishes a rate from a proportion?
o: A rate incorporates the passage of time; a proportion does not
A proportion can only describe mortality
e: A rate measures how quickly events occur per unit time. A proportion is dimensionless and time-independent beyond its stated observation window.

q: The stage of disease before any pathologic change has begun, during which host, agent and environment interact to establish susceptibility, is the:
e: The prepathogenesis period precedes the onset of pathologic change; the pathogenesis period begins once those changes start.

q: A disease with a long natural history (chronic course) will tend to show:
o: High prevalence relative to its incidence
Low prevalence relative to its incidence
Prevalence and incidence that are always equal
No relationship between prevalence and incidence
e: Because prevalence approximates incidence times average duration, a long natural history (long duration) inflates prevalence relative to incidence.

q: The basic reproduction number (R₀) is best described as:
o: The number of secondary cases in the current, partly immune population
The expected number of secondary cases from one case in a wholly susceptible population
A measure that falls as vaccination coverage rises
The incubation period of the pathogen
e: R₀ assumes complete susceptibility and is a fixed property of the pathogen and setting; it does not itself change with vaccination coverage.

q: Which reproduction number changes over the course of an outbreak as immunity and control measures accumulate?
e: R (effective reproduction number) reflects the real, currently susceptible population and moves as vaccination and control measures take effect; R₀ is fixed.

q: An epidemic curve showing a gradual rise, a broad plateau, and a gradual decline, spread over more than one incubation period, is most consistent with:
e: Continuous exposure over an extended period produces a broad hump rather than a single sharp peak (point source) or regularly-spaced waves (propagated source).

q: Ragged, irregularly-spaced clusters of cases on an epidemic curve, without the regular one-incubation-period spacing of a propagated outbreak, suggest:
e: Intermittent exposure (for example, sporadically contaminated batches) produces irregular clusters, distinguishing it from the regular spacing of person-to-person propagated spread.

q: In the CDC field-epidemiology framework for outbreak investigation, which step comes immediately before developing and testing hypotheses?
e: The sequence runs: confirm outbreak, verify diagnosis, case definition, case finding, descriptive epidemiology (person, place, time), then analytical epidemiology (hypothesis testing).

q: The three components used to build a working case definition during an outbreak investigation are:
e: A case definition is built from person (vulnerability factors), place (geographic or facility boundaries), and time (relative to exposure and onset).

q: A canine parvovirus outbreak occurs in a shelter's unvaccinated intake ward. On the morning the outbreak is identified, 40 dogs are housed in the ward and none show clinical signs. Over the next 7 days, 12 of those dogs develop confirmed parvovirus, and 2 of the 12 affected dogs die. What is the attack rate for this outbreak?
e: Attack rate is cumulative incidence over an outbreak's limited window: 12 new cases ÷ 40 at-risk dogs = 30%. 16.7% (2÷12) is the case fatality rate; 5% (2÷40) is the crude mortality rate; 12% simply restates the case count as if it were the rate.

q: A shelter cat colony has 200 cats at the start of the month, all free of ringworm. Over the following 30 days, 10 of those cats are newly diagnosed with ringworm. Separately, 3 more cats arrive already infected and go straight to isolation. What is the cumulative incidence of ringworm for the month?
e: The at-risk denominator excludes animals already infected at arrival, so CI = 10 new cases ÷ 200 at-risk cats = 5%. 6.5% wrongly counts the 3 pre-infected arrivals as new cases (13÷200); 4.9% wrongly adds them to the denominator (10÷203); 10% restates the raw case count as the rate.

q: A shelter cat room is monitored for feline URI over a 2-week period. Summed across all cats present, accounting for arrivals and departures, the room logs 500 cat-days at risk. During the same period, 10 cats develop new URI signs. What is the incidence rate, expressed per 100 cat-days?
e: Incidence rate uses animal-time at risk as its denominator: 10 ÷ 500 cat-days × 100 = 2 cases per 100 cat-days. The other options come from misplacing the decimal or from using cat count instead of cat-days as the denominator.

q: On a single day, a shelter tests all 80 cats currently in the building for FeLV. 6 cats test positive. What is the point prevalence of FeLV in this population on that day?
e: Point prevalence is existing cases at one instant: 6 ÷ 80 = 7.5%. 6% restates the case count as the rate; 13.3 per 100 cat-days wrongly applies incidence-rate units to a prevalence question; 75% is a decimal-placement error.

q: Over the course of a month, a shelter dog ward records 25 dogs with signs of kennel cough at some point during the month: 15 dogs already had signs at the start of the month, and 10 more developed new signs during the month. The ward's average daily dog population for the month is 100. What is the period prevalence of kennel cough for the month?
e: Period prevalence counts all cases, existing plus new, present at any time during the interval: 25 ÷ 100 = 25%. 10% (new cases only) is closer to cumulative incidence logic; 15% counts only the pre-existing cases; 50% uses total dogs cycled through the ward instead of average daily population.

q: During a feline panleukopenia outbreak, 22 cats are confirmed infected. Of these, 9 die from the disease. What is the case fatality rate?
e: Case fatality rate = deaths ÷ confirmed cases: 9 ÷ 22 = 40.9%. 22% and 9% each restate one raw count as the rate; 29% (9÷31) wrongly adds the deaths back into the case count before dividing.

q: Over a 3-month period, a shelter's average population is 150 animals. During this period, 22 animals are confirmed infected with canine distemper, and 6 of those infected animals die. What is the cause-specific mortality rate for canine distemper over this period?
e: Cause-specific mortality rate uses the whole population at risk as its denominator: 6 ÷ 150 = 4%. 27.3% (6÷22) is the case fatality rate; 14.7% (22÷150) is the cumulative incidence of distemper, not a mortality measure; 6% restates the death count as the rate.
